title: David Zhang
text: My name is David and this is my 7 year old son Pete. I am a 22 year old international MDS student from Minnesota in the United States. I graduated this May with a double major in computer science and financial economics. I’m hoping that the skills I’ll learn and the connections I will make at UBC will secure me a career in tech and data.

title: My first weeks in MDS
text:
Soooo my first week in MDS. I knew coming into the program that it would be a fast paced and difficult program. I did my research and found out about the 6 block program schedule ahead of time. It still didn’t do much to prepare me. So far the workload hasnt been extremely unmanageable but I am aware that as classes continue the workload will get more extreme.
On the bright side the professors are all knowledgable and there are many pleasant fellow MDS students to share the stress with together. I also have quite a view of the ocean and surrounding mountains from the 17th floor of Walter Gage North Tower.




Here’s to the next 10 months.

title: Predicting Penguin Species from Body Measurements
text:
Setup

import pandas as pd
from palmerpenguins import load_penguins
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix, accuracy_score
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

title: Predicting Penguin Species from Body Measurements
text:
Wrangling

penguins = load_penguins().dropna()

X = penguins[["bill_length_mm", "bill_depth_mm", "flipper_length_mm", "body_mass_g"]]
y = penguins["species"]

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=42
)

X_train.shape, X_test.shape

((233, 4), (100, 4))

title: Predicting Penguin Species from Body Measurements
text:
Model

from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

scaler = StandardScaler()
X_train_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X_train)
X_test_scaled = scaler.transform(X_test)

model = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)
model.fit(X_train_scaled, y_train)

preds = model.predict(X_test_scaled)
accuracy = accuracy_score(y_test, preds)

print(f"Test accuracy: {accuracy:.3f}")

Test accuracy: 0.980

title: Predicting Penguin Species from Body Measurements
text:
Figure

cm = confusion_matrix(y_test, preds, labels=model.classes_)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
im = ax.matshow(cm, cmap="Blues")

ax.set_xticks(range(len(model.classes_)))
ax.set_yticks(range(len(model.classes_)))
ax.set_xticklabels(model.classes_)
ax.set_yticklabels(model.classes_)
ax.set_xlabel("Predicted species")
ax.set_ylabel("True species")
ax.xaxis.set_label_position("top")

for i in range(cm.shape[0]):
    for j in range(cm.shape[1]):
        ax.text(j, i, str(cm[i, j]), ha="center", va="center")

plt.colorbar(im)
plt.show()







Figure 1: Confusion matrix for species classification.

title: Predicting Penguin Species from Body Measurements
text:
Findings
The model classified penguin species with a 98% accuracy on the (small)test set. Of 100 tests 2 were misclassified Chinstrap as Adelie. Gentoo penguins were classified perfectly; maybe due to their body mass and flippers being considerably heavier and longer.

penguins_clean <- penguins |> 
  drop_na()

title: How Do Penguin Species Differ?
text:
Summary Statistics

penguins_clean |> 
  group_by(species, island) |> 
  summarize(
    mean_mass = mean(body_mass_g),
    mean_flipper = mean(flipper_length_mm),
    n = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# A tibble: 5 × 5
  species   island    mean_mass mean_flipper     n
  <fct>     <fct>         <dbl>        <dbl> <int>
1 Adelie    Biscoe        3710.         189.    44
2 Adelie    Dream         3701.         190.    55
3 Adelie    Torgersen     3709.         192.    47
4 Chinstrap Dream         3733.         196.    68
5 Gentoo    Biscoe        5092.         217.   119

title: How Do Penguin Species Differ?
text:
Figure

ggplot(penguins_clean, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, color = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 2) +
  labs(
    x = "Flipper length (mm)",
    y = "Body mass (g)",
    color = "Species"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 1: Flipper length vs. body mass by species.

title: How Do Penguin Species Differ?
text:
Findings
Through this analysis we find that body mass and flipper length differ largely by species but do not differ much when it comes to what island they reside on. Adelie penguins have a consistent mean body mass around 3700g regardless of Island. Chinstrap penguins are close to Adelie in size, at roughly 3733g on average.
Gentoo penguins stand apart. With a mean body mass of about 5092g and mean flipper length of 217mm, they are noticeably heavier and longer-flippered than either Adelie or Chinstrap. They are roughly 1.4kg heavier on average than Adelie.
We see the same results showcased in our figure with Gentoo penguins clearly being on the upper right section of the grpah corresponding to higher body mass and flipper length.

title: About
text:
I was born in New Jersey and lived in China with my grandparents for 4 years. Afterwards I moved to a small rural town in southern Minnesota where I lived for 18 more years.
Prior to coming to Canada for the MDS program I studied Computer science and Financial Economics at my hometown College.
The reason why I decided to pursue a Masters in Data Science is because I became very interested in both machine learning and data; more so than computer science. My college didn’t offer a data science program which was one of the many reasons that drove me to UBC.
Outside of academics I mainly spend my time in the gym, eating, sleeping, and gaming. However I never say no to spontaneous plans with friends. I also enjoy watching football and finding random youtube fixations.
